title: Mutually reinforcing and wrong: military AI agents in the agentic interspace | The Strategist
paragraphs: Every defence force fielding AI is asking the same question: can we trust this system? It is an essential question, but no longer a sufficient one. A much more significant danger lies in already trusted systems talking to each other.

Picture three AI agents in a headquarters. One assesses intelligence, one generates courses of action, one, acting as an adversary, stress–tests the plan. Individually, each has passed accreditation. Together, they tell a commander that an adversary attack is imminent, backed by what looks like three independent confirmations. In fact, each is the same shaky assumption, passed along and re-scored – each agent treating the previous agent’s output as fresh evidence and raising its confidence – until it hardened into certainty. No agent malfunctioned. No human erred. No one is responsible.

This process happened in what I call the agentic interspace: the environment where agents exchange information and produce outcomes that cannot be traced to any single system. In it, agents read, rely on and build on one another’s outputs, usually without checking where a claim first came from or how many times it has already been counted. Small errors, biases or deliberate manipulations can therefore compound as they pass from system to system, even when every system is working exactly as designed. It is where military AI is most likely to fail, and it is not yet what most assurance methods are designed to examine.
